Clackamas County by the numbers

Where is Clackamas County, Oregon, and what is in it?

Clackamas County covers about 1,884 square miles south and east of Portland, with Oregon City as the county seat and Lake Oswego as its largest city. It belongs to the Portland-Vancouver-Hillsboro metro area and borders Multnomah, Hood River, Wasco, Marion, Yamhill and Washington counties.

The county runs from river-level suburbs to Mount Hood, which the Oregon Blue Book gives as 11,235 feet. Oregon City sits at 55 feet. Parts of Mount Hood National Forest and Willamette National Forest fall inside the county line, and Timberline Lodge draws visitors year round.

That spread matters when you sell. A house in Lake Oswego, one in Oregon City and a cabin on the Mount Hood side of the county sit in different markets and under different combinations of taxing districts, yet all of them appear on one county tax roll.

What is the history behind Clackamas County?

Clackamas started on July 5, 1843, as Clackamas District, one of the four original districts of Oregon, and became a county in 1845. It is named for the Clackamas people, a Chinookan band who lived along the Willamette, Clackamas, Sandy and Columbia rivers.

Oregon City has a long list of firsts. The Blue Book calls it the first incorporated city west of the Rocky Mountains, the first capital of the Oregon Territory and the site of the territory's first legislative session. Willamette Falls, beside the city, was an Indigenous fishing and cultural site long before the locks were built.

Per Wikipedia's county entry, the Willamette Meteorite was taken from a field near present-day West Linn in 1902. Old plats and long-held family parcels are common here, so inherited houses with unclear paperwork are not unusual.

How big is the Clackamas County economy and population?

The 2020 Census counted 421,401 residents in Clackamas County, the third-highest total in Oregon, with a median age of 41.7 and 82.9% of residents living in urban areas. Density works out to about 225 people per square mile.

The Blue Book lists the county's economic base as agriculture, metals manufacturing, trucking and warehousing, nursery stock, retail services, distribution and construction. Tourism around Mount Hood adds to that.

Oregon's own statistics show how large the property base has become. The county's assessed value reached about $66.1 billion in fiscal year 2024-25.

What does the Clackamas County climate do to a house?

Oregon City averages 48.40 inches of precipitation a year, with a January mean of 40.2 degrees Fahrenheit and a July mean of 68.4 degrees.

Homes in this climate tend to show the same set of wear points:

  • moss and worn granules on roofs, plus clogged gutters
  • wet crawl spaces and failing vapor barriers
  • decks, fences and wood siding that rot at the ground line
  • trees that overhang the roof or lean toward the structure

A house with several of these issues can be hard to list in the usual way. Some owners choose to sell it as it stands instead of paying for repairs first.

What are the Clackamas County property tax numbers at a glance?

Clackamas County taxing districts imposed about $1.17 billion in property tax for fiscal year 2024-25. The table keeps the numbers that sellers ask about most.

ItemClackamas County figure
Total assessed value, FY 2024-25$66.15 billion
Taxes imposed, FY 2024-25about $1.17 billion
Average rate per $1,000 of assessed value$17.68 (statewide $17.43)
Measure 5 rate per $1,000 of Measure 5 value$9.82
Assessment and Taxation office150 Beavercreek Road, Room 135, Oregon City
Office hoursMonday to Thursday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Phone and email503-655-8671, propertytaxinfo@clackamas.us
County Clerk (appeal petitions)503-655-8662

These come from the Department of Revenue's FY 2024-25 statistics report and the county's own pages.

Why does a Clackamas County tax bill not follow the sale price?

Oregon taxes the lower of a home's real market value and its maximum assessed value, so a rising market does not automatically raise a bill. The county's Measures 5 and 50 page explains that Measure 50 rolled each property's 1997-98 assessed value back to 90% of its 1995-96 value and then limited growth to 3% a year.

The 3% cap has exceptions for new construction, remodeling, new subdivisions and rezoning. A buyer who adds square footage can see assessed value jump on that portion.

Measure 5 works on a separate track. It caps education taxes at $5 and general government taxes at $10 per $1,000 of real market value, and anything over the cap is compressed, with local option levies cut first. The county adds that a lower market value does not lower taxes unless it falls below assessed value, so many owners see no change after a successful appeal.

How do you pay a Clackamas County tax bill, and what does it cost?

Clackamas County takes payment by mail, online, bank bill pay, in person at Room 135 in Oregon City, or in the drop box at the front of the building. The county's payment options page notes that checks must name Clackamas County Tax and that cash should not be mailed.

Online payments go through US Bank at apps.clackamas.us/pay/at, with a $3 e-check fee, 2.49% on credit cards and MasterCard debit, and $3.95 on Visa debit. Bank bill pay is handled by your bank, can take several business days and counts only when the county posts it.

The office does not accept prepayment of taxes a district has not certified, except in cases the law allows, such as recording a subdivision or moving a manufactured home. Payments go to the oldest year owed first, which matters if a seller has more than one year behind.

What happens to Clackamas County properties with unpaid taxes?

Real property tax in Clackamas County is delinquent after May 15, and foreclosure starts once taxes have been late for three years. Statements mark accounts that face foreclosure with an asterisk.

State law fills in the rest. Under ORS chapter 312, a foreclosed property is held for two years, and during that time these people can redeem it:

  • anyone who held an interest on the judgment date, and their heirs or devisees
  • anyone with a recorded lien on the property
  • a city or district with a lien on it

Redemption costs the full judgment with interest, a 5% penalty and a fee. If nobody redeems, the tax collector deeds the property to the county.

The Department of Revenue's foreclosure summary gives Clackamas figures from county records: 33 properties sold with surplus proceeds for foreclosures filed from 2017 to 2023, with potential surplus of about $1.5 million. The report calls these estimates that may change. The point for owners is that equity above the debt is at stake, not only the tax bill.

How do you appeal a Clackamas County property value?

In Clackamas County the appeal body is called the Property Value Appeals Board, and petitions go to the County Clerk by December 31. County Clerk staff at 503-655-8662 can send petition forms, and the Assessment and Taxation office at 503-655-8671 can discuss the value before you file.

Oregon's calendar from the Department of Revenue adds the structure: the board convenes on or after the first Monday in February and adjourns by March 15, and the clerk starts accepting petitions after statements go out.

Because Measure 5 and Measure 50 limit most bills, an appeal changes the bill mostly when real market value sits close to assessed value, or when the property was valued with features it does not have. Photos, an appraisal and sales near January 1 give the board something concrete.

What should a Clackamas County seller handle before closing?

Start with the tax year. Oregon's runs from July 1 to June 30, and the lien attaches on July 1, so ask the escrow officer to show how the year will be split and to verify nothing older is owed.

Second, check for a senior or disabled deferral. The state pays the county for qualifying owners and records a lien at 6% interest, and a sale or change of ownership ends the program. The balance, interest and recording costs are then due by August 15 of the following year, and heirs can be responsible.

Third, plan the seller disclosure. Under ORS 105.464 the buyer has five days to revoke after receiving it, and sales by court-appointed personal representatives and foreclosing financial institutions can claim an exclusion.

More questions about Clackamas County, OR Property Tax Guide

When are Clackamas County property taxes due?

Clackamas County bills are due November 15, February 15 and May 15, and the date shifts to the next business day when it falls on a weekend or holiday. Paying in full by November 15 earns a 3% discount.

What is the property tax rate in Clackamas County?

The average rate was $17.68 per $1,000 of assessed value in fiscal year 2024-25, according to the Oregon Department of Revenue. Your own rate depends on the taxing districts that cover your address.

How do I contact Clackamas County Assessment and Taxation?

Call 503-655-8671 or email propertytaxinfo@clackamas.us. The office is at 150 Beavercreek Road, Room 135, Oregon City, and keeps Monday to Thursday hours from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Does Clackamas County foreclose on unpaid property taxes?

Yes. Foreclosure begins after taxes have been delinquent for three years, and the owner then has a two-year redemption period after the judgment. Unredeemed property is deeded to the county.

Can I lower my Clackamas County property tax by appealing?

Sometimes. Because taxes follow the lower of market value and assessed value, a lower market value only helps if it drops below assessed value. File with the County Clerk by December 31.

What do I owe if I sell a house with a deferred property tax lien?

You owe the deferred taxes, 6% annual interest and recording costs. The state program makes the balance due by August 15 of the year after a sale or ownership change.

Lane County by the numbers

Where is Lane County, Oregon, and why is it so varied?

Lane County runs from the Pacific coast to the Cascade crest, and Eugene is the county seat. It covers 4,722 square miles, which makes it one of only two Oregon counties that reach from the ocean to the mountains. The 2020 census counted 382,971 residents, the fourth highest total in the state.

Parts of the Willamette, McKenzie and Siuslaw rivers run through it, and it holds pieces of the Umpqua, Siuslaw and Willamette National Forests. Lane County was established on January 29, 1851, and named for Joseph Lane, Oregon's first territorial governor. Eugene became the seat after the 1853 election.

About 82% of residents live in urban areas. The rest are spread across small communities such as Dexter, Marcola, Mapleton, Lorane, Blachly and McKenzie Bridge, where a house may rely on a well, a septic system and a rural fire district.

Who employs people in Lane County?

The biggest employers are PeaceHealth Medical Group, the University of Oregon, the Eugene 4J School District and the federal government. A 2017 Eugene list put PeaceHealth at 5,808 employees and the University of Oregon at 5,549, with Lane Community College at 1,650.

Springfield, the second city, has a different base. Its largest employers include PeaceHealth (3,500), the Springfield School District (1,380) and McKenzie-Willamette Medical Center (940). The Weyerhaeuser mill complex that opened there in 1949 closed its sawmill and plywood plants in the 1990s.

Tourism adds to the mix. Direct visitor spending reached $1.1 billion in 2023, and Florence on the coast (9,396 people in 2020) has a population in which about one third are retirees.

What does Lane County weather do to a house?

Wet winters are the main wear factor. Eugene averages about 40.83 inches of precipitation a year, so roofs, gutters, crawlspaces and siding see steady moisture from fall through spring. Snow is sporadic, with a median of zero inches.

The coast is wetter still. Florence averages about 75.52 inches a year, nearly twice the Willamette Valley total. Houses there need close attention to moss, decay and ventilation.

Fire has also left a mark. The Holiday Farm Fire burned from September 7 to October 29, 2020, and consumed 173,393 acres along the McKenzie River. Most structures in Blue River were destroyed, and numerous properties in nearby communities were lost. Owners of rebuilt or vacant McKenzie corridor lots often have value questions to settle with the Assessor.

How big is the Lane County property tax roll?

For 2025 to 2026, Lane County certified about $746 million in property tax, roughly 3.49% more than the year before. The roll has 182,937 accounts spread across 85 taxing districts, including cities, schools, water, fire, urban renewal, parks, libraries and ambulance districts.

The account mix shows how much of the county is residential:

  • 54.2% residential or tract property
  • 16.2% exempt
  • 9.21% commercial
  • 6.59% industrial
  • 5.46% multifamily
  • 4.17% farm and forest

Values are set as of January 1 and rest on the prior year's sales. Oregon does not reset assessed value when a house sells or is refinanced. Maximum assessed value generally rises 3% a year, and tax rate limits of $10 per $1,000 of market value for general government and $5 for schools apply, with bonds outside those caps.

Local levies change the bill by address. The 2025 statements added a new five-year Lowell Rural Fire Protection District levy of $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value, and McKenzie Rural Fire Protection District's levy rose to $1.05 from $0.60. Two houses with the same value can therefore owe different amounts.

When is Lane County property tax due?

The first payment was due November 17, 2025, because November 15 fell on a Saturday. The county's general information page gives the standard schedule: a 3% discount for paying in full by November 15, a 2% discount for paying two-thirds, and at least one-third needed to avoid interest charges.

The county posts statements online through its Assessment and Taxation pages and mails them as well. The county's website offers a property lookup that shows the account and its district breakdown. Open the account of the house you plan to sell and screenshot the balance before you talk to a buyer.

How does a Lane County value appeal work?

Start with the Assessor's Office at 541-682-4321 if the market value looks wrong. If that fails, file a petition with the Property Value Appeals Board (PVAB), which is staffed through Lane County Deeds and Records at 125 East 8th Avenue, Eugene.

  • Deadline for the 2026 tax year: December 31, 2026, at 4:00 pm for hand delivery, or postmarked by that date.
  • Filing opens the day after tax statements are mailed.
  • Fee: $35.00 per tax account, capped at $350.00 for multiple accounts with the same owner and subdivision.
  • Hearings run on Zoom, starting on or after the first Monday in February 2027 and ending by April 15, 2027.
  • Evidence must arrive at least two business days before the hearing.

PVAB hears value only. The county states that it does not hear disputes about the amount of tax billed. A further appeal goes to the Oregon Tax Court Magistrate Division within 30 days of the order. The county's own appeals page has the forms.

The board can also review values adjusted for destroyed or damaged property, which matters to owners hit by the 2020 fires.

What does recording a deed cost in Lane County?

Lane County Deeds and Records posts a fee schedule that rises on July 1, 2026. Under House Bill 3175, the Public Land Corner Preservation Fee goes from $10 to $25 per document, and the total for a one-page, one-title document moves from $87 to $102. The schedule lists deed records, deeds of trust, mortgages and easements at $102, with $5 for each added page.

Payment is by check or money order, card (with a 3% bank fee) or cash in person. Documents submitted with too little money are returned without being recorded, so build in a buffer for multi-page deeds.

What if Lane County taxes are behind or the house needs work?

Oregon law makes real property subject to tax foreclosure once three years have passed since the earliest delinquency. After judgment the county holds the property for two years, and the owner or a lienholder can redeem during that time.

Many Lane County sellers carry other problems on the way to a sale: inherited houses on rural lots, deferred roof work, tenants in place, or a lien. The practical order is the same in each case. Get the tax balance, get the lien payoff, then compare offers that do not require repairs. The state's deferral program, open to qualifying senior and disabled owners, also leaves a lien that must be paid at sale.

More questions about Lane County, OR Property Tax Guide

What is the Lane County, Oregon property tax appeal deadline?

For the 2026 tax year it is December 31, 2026, at 4:00 pm for hand delivery or postmarked by that date. File with the Property Value Appeals Board at Lane County Deeds and Records, 125 East 8th Avenue, Eugene.

How much does it cost to appeal a Lane County property value?

The fee is $35.00 per tax account. For several accounts with the same owner in one subdivision, the maximum is $350.00.

Can the appeals board lower my Lane County tax bill?

It can change property value, not the tax bill directly. The county says a lower value does not always produce a refund.

What discount does Lane County give for paying property tax early?

It gives 3% off for paying in full by November 15 and 2% for paying two-thirds. At least one-third has to be paid to avoid interest.

Does selling a Lane County house reset its assessed value?

No. Oregon does not reset values at sale or refinancing, and maximum assessed value generally rises 3% a year unless there is new construction or a similar change.

Linn County by the numbers

Where is Linn County, Oregon, and what towns does it include?

Linn County lies in the middle of the Willamette Valley, and Albany is both the county seat and the largest city. The county covers 2,309 square miles and had 128,610 residents in 2020, up 10.2% from 2010. It borders Benton, Lane, Marion, Polk, Jefferson and Deschutes counties and reaches east into the Willamette National Forest.

The Provisional Legislature created Linn County on December 28, 1847, and named it for Missouri Senator Lewis F. Linn. The seat started at Calapooia, later Brownsville, and an 1851 act moved it to Albany.

Cities and towns include Albany, Lebanon, Sweet Home, Brownsville, Harrisburg, Halsey, Scio, Tangent, Millersburg, Lyons and Sodaville, plus parts of Gates, Idanha and Mill City. About 34.2% of residents live in rural areas, so many Linn County sellers own acreage, a shop or a farm house.

What does the Linn County economy rely on?

Wood products and agriculture lead. Linn County farms grow common and perennial ryegrass and other specialty crops, the county has the only emery mine in the United States, and it produces manufactured and motor homes. Timber was once dominant: in 1990 it accounted for 40% of manufacturing jobs.

City economies differ. In Albany, retail, health care and manufacturing lead, with Oregon Freeze Dry, ATI Specialty Alloys and Components, and the 76-bed Samaritan Albany General Hospital among the named employers. In Lebanon (18,447 people at the 2020 census), Lowe's Regional Distribution Center is the largest employer at 650 jobs. In Sweet Home (9,828 people), HEVI-Shot and a timber investment firm are listed, and median household income was $43,589 in the source's data.

What does the Willamette Valley climate mean for a Linn County house?

The rainy season does most of the damage. Albany averages about 39.89 inches of precipitation a year, with December the wettest month, and roughly 5.5 inches of snow. Summers are warm and dry, with August highs near 83 degrees Fahrenheit. A 2021 record of 110 degrees (111 in the table) shows that heat spikes happen.

Sweet Home sits closer to the Cascades. Its Foster Dam station averages about 54.45 inches a year, mostly from October through March. Moss, drainage and crawlspace moisture are the usual inspection items there.

Wildfire reached the eastern edge of the county in 2020. The Santiam Fire, ignited on August 16 and contained December 10, burned 402,274 acres across Marion, Linn, Jefferson and Clackamas counties. Detroit and Gates were nearly destroyed, and Idanha and Mill City were damaged to varying degrees. More than 1,500 structures were lost.

How do people get around Linn County?

Interstate 5 and Oregon Route 99E run north and south through Albany, and U.S. Route 20 crosses it east to west. US 20 also serves Lebanon and Sweet Home, following much of the old Santiam Wagon Road, a toll road that opened in 1865 and joined the valley to central Oregon.

Albany's Amtrak station on 10th Avenue SW is served daily by the Coast Starlight, and Amtrak Cascades trains stop there several times a day.

Where does a Linn County tax dollar go?

Most of it goes to schools. In the county's notice for the 2024 assessment year, tax was split this way:

  • Schools: 41.7%
  • County: 23.5%
  • Cities: 23%
  • Rural fire districts: 7%
  • Urban renewal: 3.2%
  • Miscellaneous: 1.6%

That notice also listed voter-approved changes. Jefferson Rural Fire District added a local option levy of $0.81 per $1,000 of assessed value, Sweet Home Fire and Ambulance District set a new bond rate of $0.46 per $1,000, and a Sweet Home law enforcement levy of $7.85 per $1,000 followed two years of under-levying. A house in Sweet Home and one in Albany can therefore carry quite different rates.

How and when do you pay Linn County property tax?

Statements go out by October 25, and a full payment received by November 15 earns a 3% discount. Two-thirds paid by that date earns 2%, with the last third due May 15. The one-third plan has no discount and is paid November 15, February and May. The county sends no reminders for the February or May payments, and statements under $40 must be paid in full.

Payment options:

  • Mail a check or money order to Linn County Tax Collector, PO Box 100, Albany, OR 97321. Do not mail cash.
  • Pay in person at Room 214, Linn County Courthouse, 300 4th Avenue SW, Albany.
  • Use the drop box at the courthouse's west (Ferry Street) entrance, on the left side of the doors.
  • Pay online by card or e-check.

Postmarks are accepted for the discount, and returned checks can forfeit it. Payments are credited to the earliest year still owed.

How does Linn County handle delinquent taxes?

The Tax Collector sends delinquency notices between May 16 and May 25. A property delinquent for three years goes on the foreclosure list around July 16, the list is typically published around August 16, and final judgment follows around September 16. The county says the oldest delinquent year must be paid to remove a property from foreclosure.

Oregon's statutes then give a two-year redemption period after judgment. The state's fact sheet says an owner who redeems pays the taxes, a 5% penalty, interest and a fee, and that any surplus above the debt belongs to the owner after the county takes the property.

For a payoff figure, call 541-967-3808 during business hours. A title company will ask for it before closing on a Linn County sale.

What are the Linn County recording rules?

Linn County's Clerk records deeds from 8:30 AM to 4:00 PM at 300 4th Ave. SW in Albany. Documents received between 4:00 and 5:00 PM are recorded the next business day.

  • First page needs a blank 3 inch by 2 inch space for the recording tag and text of at least 10 point.
  • It must show the return name and address, the names of all parties, the consideration, and a "Send Tax Statements To" name and address.
  • The fee for deeds is $105.00 for the first page, plus $5.00 for each added page.
  • A document that fails first-page rules and is fixed from elsewhere in the paper costs a $20.00 non-compliance fee.

The Clerk's number is 541-967-3829.

What Linn County land rules can affect a sale?

Farm parcels deserve extra care. Oregon's special assessment for farm use values land by income instead of market value, and the Benton County guide notes that disqualified land can owe extra tax for up to 10 years, or five inside an urban growth boundary. Ending farm use, leaving an exclusive farm use zone, or approval of a nonfarm dwelling can trigger it.

The Linn County Assessor oversees these accounts, so ask for the special assessment status before you list rural land. Senior and disabled owners can also ask about the state's deferral program, which leaves a lien that is repaid at sale. The county keeps a page on it at the Senior or Disabled Citizen Deferral program.

More questions about Linn County, OR Property Tax Guide

What is the county seat of Linn County, Oregon?

Albany, which is also the largest city. An 1851 territorial act moved the seat there, and a special election in 1856 confirmed it.

When are Linn County property taxes due?

November 15 for a full payment or the first installment. The remaining installments are due February 15 and May 15, and statements are mailed by October 25.

Three years. Property delinquent that long goes on a list around July 16, and judgment follows about two months later. After that the owner has a two-year redemption period.

Douglas County by the numbers

Where is Douglas County, Oregon, and how large is it?

Douglas County is in southwest Oregon, with Roseburg as the county seat and largest city. It is the fifth-largest Oregon county by area and the largest county west of the Cascades, bordered by Lane, Klamath, Jackson, Josephine, Curry and Coos counties.

The Oregon Blue Book gives the area as about 5,071 square miles, with elevation running from sea level at the Pacific to 9,182 feet at Mount Thielsen. Almost the whole Umpqua River watershed lies inside the county, and the federal government owns more than half the land, mostly through the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management.

Towns include Sutherlin, Winchester, Myrtle Creek, Canyonville, Reedsport and Riddle, per Wikipedia. The distances between these towns are long, since the county covers more than 5,000 square miles.

How did Douglas County and its county seat develop?

Douglas County was created on January 7, 1852, from the part of Umpqua County east of the Coast Range summit, and it was named for Illinois Senator Stephen A. Douglas. Umpqua County faded after the gold rush that built it ended, and Douglas absorbed what remained in 1862.

The county seat started in Winchester in 1853. Voters moved it in 1854 to Deer Creek, renamed Roseburg in 1855. According to the Oregon State Archives, courthouses were built in Roseburg in 1855, 1870, 1891 and 1929, and the 1929 building is still in use. The county ran on a county court until 1965, when a board of commissioners took over.

The archives' history page notes that the remaining Native people were moved to reservations after the Rogue River war of 1856. Wikipedia adds that the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians descends from seven families who stayed in the hills.

What does the Douglas County economy depend on?

Forest products, mining, agriculture, fishing and recreation make up the Douglas County economy, and about a quarter of the labor force works in forest products, according to the Blue Book. The county holds nearly 1.8 million acres of commercial forest.

The Umpqua Valley wine appellation lies entirely inside the county, and Wikipedia credits HillCrest Vineyard, planted in 1961, with starting Oregon's post-Prohibition wine industry. Nickel has been refined in Riddle since 1954. The larger private employers on Wikipedia's 2015 list were:

  • Roseburg Forest Products, 1,885 employees
  • Mercy Medical Center, 1,092
  • Swanson Group Aviation, 682
  • TMS Call Center, 615
  • Seven Feathers Casino Resort, 606

Those headcounts are a decade old, so treat them as a rough guide to the employer mix and not as current staffing.

Who lives in Douglas County, and how does that affect a sale?

The 2020 Census counted 111,201 residents in Douglas County, with a median age of 48.1 and 26.8% of people aged 65 or older. About 59.6% lived in urban areas and 40.4% in rural ones, and density is about 22 people per square mile.

An older population means many owners are long-term and many homes pass through estates. Heirs who live elsewhere can face a vacant house in a small town and tax bills still addressed to the deceased owner. A property may also carry a deferral lien or a farm or forest special assessment, covered below.

What is the weather in Douglas County, and how does it treat a house?

Roseburg sits at 475 feet and receives about 33.35 inches of precipitation a year, with a January average of 41.2 degrees and a July average of 68.4, per the Blue Book. Winters are mild and wet, and summers are warm.

Houses on forested or hillside lots can have specific upkeep needs:

  • roofs and gutters that collect needles and leaves
  • decks, stairs and retaining walls on sloped ground
  • septic systems and wells on rural parcels
  • fire-season clearance around buildings near timber

Anyone selling a rural Douglas County house should ask the county what permits and records exist for the septic system and any outbuildings.

The numbers are from the Department of Revenue report and the Douglas County Assessor and Tax Office site. The low average rate reflects the combination of taxing districts here, so a bill still depends on your specific address.

How do you pay a Douglas County property tax bill?

Douglas County taxes can be paid in person, by mail or online, and the county moves a due date that lands on a weekend to the next business day. Online card payments must finish by 11:59 p.m. Pacific on the due date.

Several details come from the county's own page:

  • account numbers carry a letter prefix, R, M, U or P, such as R12345
  • a yellow statement means a mortgage company or the deferral program asked for the tax information
  • online fees are 2.49% for credit cards, $3.95 for debit and $3.00 for e-checks, and one account can be paid per transaction
  • checks go to Douglas County, with no cash by mail and no post-dated checks
  • properties in tax foreclosure or bankruptcy cannot pay online

When more than one year is owed, payments apply to the earliest year first. Tax Office hours run Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with a closure from noon to 1 p.m. The Assessor's hours are shorter, with Wednesday open only until noon and other days by appointment, so call 541-440-4222 before you drive in. The tax collector's mailing address is PO Box 8403, Medford, OR 97501.

What happens when Douglas County taxes go unpaid?

Oregon law lets a county foreclose on real property after taxes have been delinquent for three years, and a foreclosed owner then has two years to redeem. ORS chapter 312 states that holders of a recorded interest, their heirs and lien holders may redeem by paying the judgment amount, interest, a 5% penalty and a fee.

The state's calendar puts the foreclosure steps in the late summer after the third year: a list is prepared in July, published and sent to the district attorney by mid-August, and the district attorney seeks a judgment by September 16.

Interest on late taxes in Douglas County runs at 1.333% a month. For a specific account, call the Tax Office at 541-440-4253.

How do you appeal a Douglas County property value?

An appeal goes to the county's Property Value Appeals Board, and the petition is due by December 31, with the next business day used if that date falls on a weekend. The Department of Revenue calendar shows the board meeting on or after the first Monday in February and adjourning by March 15.

The Douglas County Assessor's page covers valuation and special programs but does not describe the appeal process, so the Assessor at 541-440-4222 is the first call. The office's stated duties include estimating market value for each property and managing farm, forest and exemption programs.

What should a Douglas County seller know about special assessments, deferral and disclosure?

Forest and farm land can carry a lower special assessment, and leaving the program can cost money. Benton County's Assessment FAQ notes that disqualification triggers a recovery penalty reaching back up to five years for most land and up to ten for EFU, MPA and STF land. Ask the Assessor before you split or change the use of a parcel.

Seniors may be in the state deferral program, which places a lien at 6% interest. A sale ends the deferral, and the balance is due by August 15 of the following year. The 2025 program sheet also warns that heirs can be liable.

The disclosure form under ORS 105.464 goes out with a written offer, and the buyer has five days to revoke it. Personal representatives and foreclosing financial institutions can claim an exclusion and complete only part of the form.

They are due November 15, February 15 and May 15. When the 15th falls on a weekend, the due date moves to the first business day of the next week.

Late interest is 1.333% a month, which is 16% a year. Payments apply to the earliest tax year first when more than one year is owed.

Where is the Douglas County Tax Office?

The Tax Office is at 1036 SE Douglas Ave, room CH205, in Roseburg, and the phone is 541-440-4253. It is open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and closes from noon to 1 p.m.

What is the average property tax rate in Douglas County?

The average was $11.07 per $1,000 of assessed value in fiscal year 2024-25, according to the Oregon Department of Revenue. The statewide average was $17.43.

Can I pay a Douglas County tax bill online?

Yes, by searching your property on the county site and choosing Pay My Bills. Fees apply, and properties in tax foreclosure or bankruptcy cannot be paid online.

What happens to a tax deferral lien if I sell my Douglas County home?

The deferred taxes, 6% interest and recording costs come due after a sale. Payment is due by August 15 of the next year.

Jackson County by the numbers

Where is Jackson County, Oregon, and how did it take shape?

Jackson County sits in southern Oregon along the California line, and Medford is its seat. The county covers 2,802 square miles, and the 2020 census counted 223,259 people. Most of them live in the Rogue Valley, along the Bear Creek corridor that links Ashland, Talent, Phoenix, Medford and Central Point.

The Territorial Legislature created the county on January 12, 1852, and named it for President Andrew Jackson. Gold drew the first wave of settlers that year. Jacksonville was the first county seat, designated in 1853. The railroad built in the 1880s ran through Medford instead, and the seat moved there in 1927.

The county has 11 incorporated cities and 34 unincorporated communities, so a Jackson County home can sit inside a city, in a small community with its own fire district, or on rural land outside any city. That mix matters for a seller, because the taxing districts on the bill change from one address to the next.

What drives the Jackson County economy?

Health care leads. Asante Rogue Regional Medical Center and Providence Medford Medical Center together employ more than 2,000 people, and Harry and David is described as the largest employer in southern Oregon, with about 1,700 year-round workers and 6,700 seasonal ones. Lithia Motors has been headquartered in Medford since 1970.

Outside Medford the picture shifts:

  • Central Point (18,997 people in 2020) lists School District 6 and Costco among its top employers, and its farms are dominated by pears and wine grapes.
  • Ashland (21,360 people in 2020) leans on Southern Oregon University and the Oregon Shakespeare Festival, which runs February to October.
  • Jacksonville (3,020 people in 2020) holds a historic district with more than 100 buildings, designated a National Historic Landmark in 1966.

For a seller, this spread means buyers for a Jackson County house come from hospital staff, university households, retirees and orchard or vineyard owners. Condition and location still drive the price more than any single employer.

What does the Rogue Valley climate mean for a house?

Medford has a dry Mediterranean climate, and the wear on a roof and cooling system shows it. The city averages about 61 afternoons above 90 degrees Fahrenheit and 11 above 100 each year, with a record of 115 degrees set in July 1946 and matched in June 2021. Annual precipitation is only about 18.43 inches.

Winter is mild but not frost free. Medford sees freezing mornings on roughly 64 days a year and about 3.4 inches of snow on average. Ashland, at 1,949 feet, gets about 20 inches of precipitation and 1.4 inches of snow.

The larger risk is fire. The Almeda Drive Fire started on September 8, 2020, near Ashland and reached Phoenix and Talent within hours. It burned about 3,200 acres, destroyed more than 3,000 structures and was contained on September 15. Houses that were damaged, rebuilt or left vacant afterward often come with unusual tax and insurance questions.

If your Jackson County property was damaged, ask the Assessor's Office how the loss is reflected in its value before you set a price.

Which Jackson County office does what with property tax?

Two offices share the work. The Assessor's Office values property, keeps the maps and ownership records, handles exemptions and oversees farm and forest special assessments. The Taxation office in the Finance Department collects the money.

The Assessor's Office values residential, commercial and business personal property, plus industrial land and improvements under $1,000,000. It also verifies sales to track the market. Reach it at 541-774-6059 or Assessor@jacksoncountyor.gov. The county also posts a Summary of Assessment and Levies report each fall, with dated PDFs for 2025 and 2026.

The Taxation office takes payments in Room 111A at 10 S Oakdale Ave. Its counter hours are Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 4 PM, and its email is taxation@jacksoncountyor.gov.

When are Jackson County property taxes due, and what do you save by paying early?

The first payment is due November 15, and paying in full by then earns a 3% discount. The county's 2026 to 2027 schedule says statements go out by October 25, and a weekend or holiday due date moves to the next business day. In 2026 the 15th falls on a Sunday, so Monday, November 16 is the date to confirm with the office.

  • Full payment by November 15: 3% discount.
  • Two-thirds by November 15: 2% discount, with the rest due May 15.
  • One-third by November 15: no discount, with more due February 15 and May 15.
  • Interest of 1.333% a month (16% a year) starts on December 16, February 16 and May 16 for the three installments.

A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before the due date, and the county warns that local postmarks may not be applied because of mail consolidation. Drop boxes are open around the clock, and payments there are credited the same day. Payments go first to fees, then to the oldest tax year owed.

Online card payments carry a third-party fee of 2.40% (minimum $2.00). Debit is 1% (minimum $2.00) and e-check is $2.50. The county keeps none of it. Phone payments go through 541-774-6541. Prepayment is generally refused, except for omitted property or estimated tax on a new partition, plat or subdivision.

How do you appeal a Jackson County property value?

You file a petition with the Property Value Appeals Board clerk in Jackson County after you receive your tax statement and no later than December 31. If December 31 lands on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

From there the Oregon Tax Court, Magistrate Division, is the next stop. A value appeal from a board order must be filed within 30 days of the order. Appeals about exemptions, special assessment disqualification or omitted property have a 90 day window. The Magistrate Division is at 1163 State St, Salem, and the state's appeals page lists the rules.

An appeal changes value only. It does not erase a bill that is already due, so a seller facing a closing date should pay what the county asks and treat any refund as a later matter.

What happens when Jackson County taxes go unpaid?

The county mails delinquent notices in mid-June, and interest runs at 1.333% a month on each missed installment. Real property becomes subject to foreclosure once three years have passed since the earliest delinquency date, under ORS 312.010.

After a foreclosure judgment, the county holds the property for two years. During that time the owner or a lienholder can redeem by paying the judgment amount, interest, a 5% penalty and a fee. Oregon's foreclosure fact sheet also says that if the property is worth more than what is owed, the owner is entitled to the surplus after the county takes it.

Selling is one way to stop that clock. A cash sale can pay the old years out of proceeds at closing, and the Taxation office at 541-774-6541 can give you the balance for each year.

What does it cost to record a deed in Jackson County?

Jackson County's posted schedule lists $99.00 for a one-page deed (bargain and sale, quitclaim, warranty or transfer on death), with $5.00 for each added page. A trust deed or mortgage is $116.00. The schedule was revised January 19, 2024, so call the Clerk at 541-774-6152 to confirm today's number.

A document missing required first-page information carries a $20.00 non-standard fee. Regular copies are $4.00 for the first page, and certified copies are $7.75.

What should a Jackson County seller check before closing?

Start with the tax account, then the land. A few checks save the most trouble:

  • Pull the balance for every open year from the Taxation office.
  • Confirm whether the parcel has a farm or forest special assessment, since ending that use can trigger extra tax.
  • Ask whether any special assessment, fee or charge is attached to the account.
  • For fire-damaged or rebuilt property, ask the Assessor how the value was set.

Oregon's farm-use guidance says disqualified land can owe additional tax for up to 10 years, or five years inside an urban growth boundary. Rogue Valley orchard and vineyard parcels are exactly the type of land this affects.

Seniors and disabled owners sometimes use the state deferral program. The Department of Revenue pays the county on the owner's behalf and records a lien, which must be repaid, with 6% simple interest, before it is released. A deferral account therefore has a payoff figure at closing, and the state says release takes about eight weeks after payment posts.

What is the county seat of Jackson County, Oregon?

Medford. Jacksonville was the first seat in 1853, and the seat moved to Medford in 1927 after the railroad bypassed Jacksonville.

How much is the early payment discount on Jackson County property tax?

It is 3% for paying in full by November 15, and 2% for paying two-thirds by that date. The one-third plan has no discount, and the county says to confirm the exact due date with the Taxation office when the 15th falls on a weekend.

What is the Jackson County property tax appeal deadline?

December 31, filed with the Property Value Appeals Board after you receive your statement. If that date is a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies.

Where do I pay Jackson County property tax in person?

At Room 111A, 10 S Oakdale Ave, Medford, Monday through Friday from 8 AM to 4 PM. Drop boxes are open 24 hours a day, and the phone number is 541-774-6541.

Can I sell a Jackson County house with back taxes owed?

Yes. The unpaid years are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Call the Taxation office for the balance of each year, because payments are applied to the oldest year first and interest is 1.333% a month.

Where is Jefferson County, Oregon?

Jefferson County is a high-desert county in central Oregon, and Madras is the county seat. It covers 1,791 square miles and had 24,502 residents at the 2020 census, a 12.8% rise from 2010. The county was created on December 12, 1914, from part of Crook County and takes its name from Mount Jefferson, Oregon's second tallest mountain.

It borders Marion, Wasco, Wheeler, Crook, Deschutes and Linn counties. Madras was incorporated in 1911 and became the permanent seat after a 1916 general election. Culver, the first temporary seat, had 1,602 residents in 2020.

Two large blocks of land shape what a seller can own here. The Warm Springs reservation, owned by the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs, covers about 21% of county land. The U.S. Forest Service manages about 24%. Owners of any parcel near those boundaries should confirm the tax status of the land with the Assessor.

What are the main communities in Jefferson County?

Madras is the commercial center, with 7,456 residents in 2020. U.S. 97 and U.S. 26 meet there, and 97 is split into a one-way pair through town. Madras Municipal Airport sits on the former Madras Army Air Field.

The largest unincorporated community is Crooked River Ranch, a census-designated place of 4,912 people in southern Jefferson County between the Deschutes and Crooked rivers, near Lake Billy Chinook. The ranch covers about 12,000 acres and is described as the largest homeowner association in Oregon. It was bought in 1910 by Harry V. Gates, developed as a recreational site in 1972, and rezoned as a residential subdivision in 1992.

That history matters to a seller. A Crooked River Ranch house comes with HOA rules and dues, so ask for the association's documents early.

What does the Jefferson County economy rest on?

Agriculture is the main source of income. The county grows vegetable, grass and flower seeds, garlic, mint and sugar beets on about 60,000 acres of irrigated land, and it has large rangelands. Irrigation projects developed in the late 1930s, and the 1911 railroad linked Madras to the Columbia River.

The forest products industry operated until 2016, and the Warm Springs Forest Products complex was the largest single industry. On the reservation, the Warm Springs hydroelectric projects on the Deschutes River are the tribes' largest revenue source, and the Indian Head Casino opened on U.S. 26 in 2012.

Tourism adds fishing, hunting, camping, boating and rock hunting. The Cove Palisades State Park, on Lake Billy Chinook where the Crooked, Deschutes and Metolius rivers meet, offers two campgrounds and rental cabins. Round Butte Dam was completed on the Deschutes in 1964.

What is the weather like, and what does it do to a house?

Madras is dry and cold at night. It averages only 9.56 inches of precipitation a year, about 12.1 inches of snow, a July mean high of 87.1 degrees Fahrenheit and a January mean low of 22.1. The record high is 112 and the record low is minus 45. The county as a whole gets about 300 days of sunshine a year.

  • With so little rain, sun exposure and wide temperature swings are the main stresses on roofs and siding.
  • Hard freezes make pipe and well protection a real maintenance item.
  • Wildfire is a regional concern. The 2020 Santiam Fire burned in Jefferson County as well as Marion, Linn and Clackamas.

Who collects property tax in Jefferson County?

The Finance Department bills and collects property tax for every taxing district in the county. Its office is at 66 SE D Street, Suite E, Madras, and the Assessor is a separate department listed in the county's navigation. The county's tax collection pages cover forms, a mailing address change form, the tax statement guide, foreclosure information and an appeal guide titled How to Appeal Your Property Value.

Oregon's tax year runs July 1 to June 30. Statements go out by October 25, and the three installments are due November 15, February 15 and May 15. A weekend or holiday date rolls to the next business day.

How do payment timing and discounts work in Jefferson County?

Discounts come from ORS 311.505. Pay in full by the November due date and you save 3%. Pay two-thirds and you save 2%. Pay less than two-thirds and there is no discount.

Timing rules are written for mail and online payers differently:

  • By mail, a USPS postmark on or before the due date counts as timely under ORS 305.820. The check goes to Jefferson County Tax.
  • With no postmark, the delivery date is used.
  • Online bill pay usually has no postmark, so the money has to arrive by the due date.
  • Online payments through Point and Pay count if sent by 11:59 pm on the 15th.

Card payments cost 2.50% (minimum $2.00), a Visa Signature debit card costs $3.95, and an eCheck costs $1.50. The county does not keep any fee. The phone number for card payments is 1-877-865-0432, and in-person payment accepts cash, check, money order or card.

Overdue taxes carry 1.33% interest a month, which is 16% a year, posting on the 16th of each month.

What can you do if Jefferson County says your house is worth too much?

Use the county's appeal guide first, then file with the Property Value Appeals Board by December 31. The Department of Revenue's page says to file after you receive your tax statement, with a weekend or holiday deadline moving to the next business day.

If the board's order does not fix it, the Oregon Tax Court Magistrate Division takes value appeals filed within 30 days of the order. Exemption denials and special assessment disqualification have a 90 day window. The county's own pages did not state the board's deadline, so confirm the current date with the Finance Department at 541-475-4458.

What if a Jefferson County owner is behind on taxes?

Oregon sets one rule for every county. Real property can be foreclosed once three years have passed since the earliest delinquency date. The list is prepared in July and published in August, and the state's fact sheet says paying the full tax and interest removes the property, with a 5% penalty added after publication.

After judgment the redemption period is two years. The owner, an heir, a recorded lienholder or a city with a lien may redeem by paying the taxes, interest, the penalty and a fee. If the house is worth more than the debt, the owner is entitled to the surplus.

Ask the Finance Department for a balance by year, and share it with the buyer's title company so that escrow can pay the oldest years first.

What should a Jefferson County seller prepare?

Gather four things before you ask for offers. They are the latest tax statement, the well and septic records for a rural lot, the HOA documents if the home is in Crooked River Ranch, and the special assessment status of any farm acreage.

Farm acreage needs special care. Oregon's farm-use rules allow additional tax for up to 10 years when land is disqualified, or five years inside an urban growth boundary.

More questions about Jefferson County, OR Property Tax Guide

What is the county seat of Jefferson County, Oregon?

Madras. It was incorporated in 1911 and became the permanent seat after a 1916 election, replacing Culver as the temporary seat.

Where do I pay Jefferson County property tax?

At the Finance Department, 66 SE D Street, Suite E, Madras, or by mail, phone (1-877-865-0432) or online through Point and Pay. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

How much discount does Jefferson County give for early payment?

3% for paying in full by the November due date and 2% for paying two-thirds. Paying less than two-thirds earns no discount.

What interest does Jefferson County charge on late property tax?

1.33% per month, or 16% a year, posting on the 16th of each month until paid.

Can I sell a Jefferson County house that has unpaid property tax?

Yes. The unpaid amount is settled from the sale proceeds at closing. Get a balance by year from the Finance Department so the title company can pay the oldest years first.

Benton County by the numbers

Where is Benton County, Oregon, and how is it laid out?

Benton County sits in the Willamette Valley and covers 679 square miles, which makes it the fourth-smallest Oregon county by land area. Corvallis is both the county seat and the largest city.

The other incorporated places are Adair Village, Monroe and Philomath, plus a slice of Albany that crosses over from Linn County. Polk County lies to the north, Lincoln to the west, Linn to the east and Lane to the south.

The Oregon Blue Book puts Corvallis at 224 feet above sea level. It also names Mary's Peak, McDonald Forest, Alsea Falls and the William L. Finley National Wildlife Refuge among the county's landmarks.

How did Benton County begin, and why does it still matter to owners?

The Provisional Government of Oregon created Benton County on December 23, 1847, and named it for Missouri Senator Thomas Hart Benton. The original county was far larger than today's version, and the Blue Book notes that pieces of it later became Coos, Curry, Douglas, Jackson, Josephine, Lane and Lincoln counties.

The settlement first called Marysville became Corvallis and took over as county seat in 1851. In 1862 the town became home to the Oregon State Agricultural College, now Oregon State University. The county has been a home rule county since 1972, according to Wikipedia's county entry.

What drives the Benton County economy?

Oregon State University, agriculture, forest products, research and development, electronics and wineries make up the economic base the Blue Book describes for Benton County. The university alone carries a large share of the research in forestry, agriculture and engineering.

Oregon State reported preliminary fall 2024 enrollment of 37,900 students, with 24,900 of them on the Corvallis campus, in a university news release. The 2020 Census put the county's median age at 33.2 years, and 80.6% of residents lived in an urban area.

Houses near campus often pass through landlords, estates and families who live elsewhere, so sellers here regularly deal with tenants and out-of-town heirs.

What is the weather in Benton County, and what does it do to a house?

Corvallis averages 42.71 inches of precipitation a year, with a January average of 39.3 degrees Fahrenheit and a July average of 65.6 degrees, per the Oregon Blue Book. That is a wet, mild valley climate with cool winters and no extreme heat in an average July.

Wet winters put a few parts of a house under steady strain. Buyers and their inspectors usually look first at:

  • the roof surface, flashing and gutters, where water finds the weak spots
  • crawl space moisture and the condition of floor framing and insulation
  • siding, window trim and decks that stay damp for months
  • drainage around the foundation and the lot's grading

What are the key Benton County property tax numbers?

Benton County property owners paid a county-wide total of about $198.5 million in property tax for fiscal year 2024-25, according to the Oregon Department of Revenue. The table below collects the figures that matter most when you read a bill or plan a sale.

ItemBenton County figure

Taxes imposed, FY 2024-25about $198.5 million

Statements mailed byOctober 25
Installment datesNovember 15, February 15, May 15
Appeal petition deadlineDecember 31 (next business day if a weekend)
Appeal hearing windowfirst Monday in February through April 15
Tax Office phone541-766-6808
Assessment Department phone541-766-6855

The figures come from the Department of Revenue's FY 2024-25 statistics report and from the county's own pages.

How does Benton County calculate a property tax bill?

The Benton County Assessor gives every property a real market value, then taxes the lower of that number and a maximum assessed value. The county's Assessment FAQ explains that the maximum assessed value started from the 1995-96 value less 10% and can rise no more than 3% a year, plus any value from new improvements.

Nothing in that formula resets the maximum assessed value when a house changes hands, so two similar homes can carry very different bills. Tax rates are charged per $1,000 of assessed value and vary by taxing district.

Oregon also limits what a single account can owe. Measure 5 caps education taxes at $5 per $1,000 of real market value and general government taxes at $10 per $1,000. When a bill goes over the cap it is reduced, which Oregon calls compression.

When are Benton County property taxes due, and where can you pay?

Benton County taxes are due in full on November 15, or in three installments on November 15, February 15 and May 15. Paying the full amount by the November date earns a 3% discount, while installment payers get none.

When the 15th lands on a weekend, the due date moves forward. For the 2025 bills the county set the postmark deadline at November 17. Late amounts pick up 1.333% interest on the 16th of each month, as the Benton County Tax Department explains.

Ways to pay, according to the county's 2025 statement announcement:

  • the drop box in the Kalapuya Building parking lot at 4500 SW Research Way, Corvallis
  • the Tax Office on the building's first floor
  • mail to P.O. Box 964, Corvallis, OR 97339, with the payment coupon
  • online by credit card, debit card or electronic check
  • by phone at 1-866-898-2918

What happens in Benton County if taxes go unpaid?

In Benton County, unpaid real property tax is delinquent after May 15, and the county can foreclose once the first delinquency is three years old. The Tax Department's foreclosure page lays out the steps in order:

  • After May 15, delinquency notices go out and interest keeps accruing.
  • After June 15, a courtesy notice lists payment dates that avoid publication.
  • After July 15, a foreclosure notice is sent. July 15 is also the last day the office takes a personal check.
  • In mid to late August, the list of properties is published in the local paper.
  • Roughly 30 days after publication a general judgment is filed with the Circuit Court. An owner who disagrees has 30 days to answer.

Once the judgment is granted, a two-year redemption period starts. To redeem, the owner pays the taxes and interest in the judgment, a 5% penalty and 9% annual interest on the judgment period. The county does not accept partial payments, and the owner keeps possession during the period. Heirs, lienholders of record and anyone with a recorded interest on the judgment date may redeem. If nobody does, the Tax Collector deeds the property to Benton County, which may sell it at public auction.

The state rules behind this are in ORS chapter 312.

How do you appeal a Benton County property value?

You appeal to the Property Value Appeals Board, often called BOPTA, by filing a petition with the County Clerk between the day statements are mailed and December 31. If December 31 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

The county's PVAB quick reference lists these filing routes:

  • hand delivery to the County Clerk at 4500 SW Research Way, 2nd floor, by 5 p.m. on the deadline
  • mail to P.O. Box 888, Corvallis, OR 97339, postmarked by the deadline
  • fax or email (Bopta@bentoncountyor.gov) received by midnight on the deadline

The petitioner has the burden of showing the Assessor's value is wrong. Useful evidence for a house includes an arm's-length sale within roughly three to six months of January 1, a recent fee appraisal, adjusted comparable sales or repair estimates. Comparing your bill to a neighbor's does not count.

The Board meets from the first Monday in February and finishes by April 15. If you disagree with the order, you have 30 days from its mailing to file with the Oregon Tax Court Magistrate Division.

What should a Benton County seller know about taxes at closing?

Oregon's property tax year runs from July 1 to June 30, and the lien date is July 1, according to the Department of Revenue's tax calendar. Ask the escrow officer how the current year will be split between you and the buyer, and ask for a written payoff if any prior year is unpaid.

Two other items surface often with older owners. The first is the state's senior and disabled deferral program, where the state pays the county and records a lien that carries 6% interest. The balance becomes due when the home is sold or ownership changes, with payment due by August 15 of the following year, and heirs can be liable.

The second is the seller disclosure form. Under ORS 105.464, a seller delivers it with a written offer, and the buyer has five days to revoke. Sales by court-appointed personal representatives and by financial institutions that took a property through foreclosure are exempt from the full form.

More questions about Benton County, OR Property Tax Guide

When are Benton County property taxes due?

Benton County taxes are due November 15 in full, or in installments on November 15, February 15 and May 15. A full payment by November 15 earns a 3% discount, and anything unpaid after May 15 is delinquent.

How long do I have to appeal my Benton County assessment?

You can file from the day statements are mailed until December 31, or the next business day if that date is a weekend or holiday. Petitions go to the County Clerk, and hearings run from the first Monday in February to April 15.

Can Benton County foreclose on my house for unpaid taxes?

Yes, once the taxes have been delinquent for three years. After a general judgment, the owner has a two-year redemption period, and the county may deed and auction the property if nobody redeems.

Who sets the tax rate on a Benton County home?

The taxing districts set the rates, not the Assessor. The Assessment Department only assigns the property's market value and assessed value, and the Tax Office sends and collects the bills.

What happens to a senior property tax deferral when the house sells?

The deferred taxes, 6% annual interest and recording costs come due after a sale or change of ownership. Payment is due by August 15 of the following year, and the lien stays until it is paid.

Who do I call about a Benton County property tax question?

Call the Tax Office at 541-766-6808 for bills and payments, and the Assessment Department at 541-766-6855 for value questions. Both offices are open weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Deschutes County by the numbers

Where is Deschutes County, Oregon, and what shapes the land?

Deschutes County is a high desert county in Central Oregon, covering 3,055 square miles with Bend as both the county seat and the largest city. It touches Linn, Jefferson, Crook, Harney, Lake, Klamath and Lane counties.

The land is volcanic. Newberry Volcano south of Bend produced most of the lava flows, and the county holds more than 500 known caves, the most of any Oregon county, per Wikipedia's county entry. The Three Sisters, Mount Bachelor and Broken Top rise on the western edge, and the U.S. Forest Service owns 51% of the county's land.

That last number explains a lot about local property. With more than half the county in federal hands, privately owned land is limited, and it is spread across cities such as Bend, Redmond and Sisters and the rural areas between them.

How did Deschutes County come to exist?

Deschutes County was carved from the southern part of Crook County on December 13, 1916, and was the last county established in Oregon. Bend has been the seat since the beginning.

The name comes from the Deschutes River. French-Canadian trappers working for the Hudson's Bay Company called it the "Rivière des Chutes," or River of the Falls, as the Oregon Blue Book explains.

Zoning on rural land is handled by the county's Community Development Department. What a parcel allows a buyer to build or rent is worth confirming before a sale, since it can change what the property is worth to them.

What are the main employers and industries in Deschutes County?

The Blue Book lists tourism, retail trade, forest products, recreational equipment, aviation, and software and high technology as the county's economic base. Lumber, ranching and potato farming also appear in the history, and the Shevlin-Hixon Lumber Company once milled ponderosa pine around Bend.

Resorts matter to the tax base. Sunriver, Eagle Crest and Pronghorn are among the county's ten largest taxpayers, and Wikipedia notes that four destination resorts are major employers. The Blue Book also lists Redmond Airport and Central Oregon Community College among the county's features.

The population grew from 115,367 in 2000 to 198,253 in 2020, and Wikipedia's 2025 estimate is 213,072.

How cold and dry is Deschutes County, and what does it mean for a house?

Bend sits at 3,628 feet and gets about 12 inches of precipitation a year, with average temperatures of 30.5 in January and 65.5 in July, according to the Blue Book. That is a dry, high-elevation climate with real winters.

Homes face a different set of stresses than in western Oregon:

  • snow load on roofs and ice dams along the eaves
  • freeze and thaw cycles that crack driveways, patios and foundations
  • wood decks and siding that dry and split in the summer sun
  • heating systems and well or septic equipment that must handle cold snaps

A vacant house that went through a winter without heat can need real work before a lender will finance a buyer's purchase of it.

How do you read and pay a Deschutes County tax bill?

Deschutes County posts statements online in its Dial system by October 20 and mails them by October 25, and the Property Tax office asks owners to update a mailing address before September 30. A paper statement includes instructions for switching to email.

A color code helps with escrow. According to the county's tax newsletter, a yellow statement means a lender is paying the taxes and a green one means no lender is.

The county's FY 2024-25 newsletter listed these payment routes, so confirm current fees before paying:

  • mail to Deschutes County Tax Collector, PO Box 7559, Bend, OR 97708-7559
  • online at deschutes.org/tax, or by phone at (866) 871-5856 at any hour
  • a 24-hour drop box at 1300 NW Wall Street in Bend, and a Redmond box at 411 SW 9th Street open only in set windows before each due date
  • bank bill pay, with a separate payment for each account using its six-digit account number

The newsletter also advises keeping a hand-stamped USPS receipt, because mail postmarks are applied at a distribution center, and scheduling bank payments well ahead because they can arrive days late.

What can go wrong with unpaid taxes in Deschutes County?

Oregon allows tax foreclosure on real property after three years of delinquency, and the county then holds the property for two years while the owner and lienholders can redeem it. ORS chapter 312 sets those periods, a 5% penalty and a redemption fee.

Deschutes County has sold foreclosed properties at auction. The Department of Revenue's foreclosure summary records these results:

  • 2018: 37 parcels, $1,115,060
  • 2019: 34 parcels, $640,100
  • 2020: 30 parcels, $768,100
  • 2021: 12 parcels, $1,336,000
  • 2022: 16 parcels, $702,600

The summary does not report surplus for Deschutes, so it is not clear what former owners recovered. An owner who is behind has the most options before the three-year mark arrives.

How do you appeal a Deschutes County property value?

In Deschutes County, appeals go to the County Clerk's Office, which is the only office that can accept petitions. The county's appeal deadline page lists a mailing address at P.O. Box 6005, Bend, OR 97708-6005 and a delivery address at 1300 NW Wall Street, Suite 202, and says postmarks are acceptable.

State law sets the deadline at December 31, and the county's page for the 2023-24 year showed January 2, 2024, a date that fits the weekend and New Year's holiday that followed December 31 that year. The Department of Revenue's calendar has the board meeting from the first Monday in February to March 15.

For value questions before you file, the Assessor's Office takes calls at 541-388-6508 or email at appraisal@deschutes.org. The Dial site also offers a tax estimator and a rate lookup by account.

What should a Deschutes County seller know about rentals, deferral and disclosure?

Some Deschutes County houses are run as short-term rentals. In unincorporated Deschutes County, transient room tax rules in County Code Chapter 4.08 apply to overnight rentals of up to 30 consecutive days, and the county's short-term rental FAQ says paying that tax is not land use approval.

The FAQ adds that any structure used as a rental must meet land use, building and onsite wastewater rules, and that eligibility can depend on whether the dwelling was lawfully established. Sellers who run a rental should confirm the status with the Community Development Department before listing it as one.

Older owners may have a senior or disabled deferral. When the home sells, the balance with 6% interest is due by August 15 of the next year. The state's 2025 program sheet puts the late-filing fee at 10% of the last tax bill, from $20 to $180.

Finally, ORS 105.464 requires the seller disclosure with a written offer, and the buyer has five days to revoke.

When do Deschutes County property tax statements come out?

Statements for 2026-27 appear online in Dial by October 20 and are mailed by October 25. The county asks owners to fix a wrong mailing address by September 30.

Where do I pay property taxes in Deschutes County?

You can pay online at deschutes.org/tax, by phone, by mail to PO Box 7559, Bend, in a drop box or in person at 1300 NW Wall Street, Suite 203. Weekday hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

What does a yellow property tax statement mean in Deschutes County?

A yellow statement means a lender is paying the taxes through an escrow account, and a green one means no lender is. The county's newsletter uses these colors to help owners check who pays.

How do I appeal my Deschutes County assessment?

File a petition with the County Clerk at 1300 NW Wall Street, Suite 202, or by mail to PO Box 6005, Bend. The state deadline is December 31, moved to the next business day when it falls on a weekend or holiday.

Is the Deschutes County tax rate higher than the Oregon average?

No. The Department of Revenue shows an average of $16.61 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2024-25, below the statewide average of $17.43.

Do short-term rental owners in Deschutes County owe a lodging tax?

Owners of overnight rentals in unincorporated areas owe the transient room tax under County Code Chapter 4.08. Paying it does not give land use approval, so a separate review may still apply.
